newsitem.title: THAILAND: Finance minister post a hot seat in Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Finance minister post a hot seat in Thailand.

text.p: Being finance minister in crisis-hit Thailand is not easy.
The country has had five finance ministers in three administrations since 1995.
Part of the problem was that the ministers were not elected politicians and were usually appointees of fractious coalition governments, the analysts said on Friday.
Without the backing of a party or powerful allies, non-elected finance ministers were particularly vulnerable to political pressure and rivalry from coalition figures, the analysts said.

On Thursday, the respected Amnuay Viravan became the latest finance minister to quit after less than seven months in the post. He resigned over differences with political rivals in the six-party coalition government of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh.
The government is set to appoint Thanong Bidaya, the low-profile president of Thai Military Bank Plc, to be Amnuay's successor on Friday, political sources said.
The poor recent track record for finance ministers has seriously rattled foreign investor confidence in Thailand, which is suffering its worst economic slump in more than a decade, analysts said.

Thailand's once-booming economy is in tatters: exports have fallen, the ailing finance sector is over-exposed to depressed property firms, the stock market is at an eight-year low and the baht has been under attack.
"Investors want to see stability in the job. Someone with stature, a track record and credibility," said Sriyan Pietersz, head of research at Capital Nomura Securities.

Given that Thailand is being run by a coalition government, a non-political figure as finance minister would inevitably run into trouble again with powerful politicians and their vested business interests, analysts said.

"It's a difficult situation for the finance minister if he is not a politician. The only hope for the country is that politicians themselves understand the situation. They must accommodate measures that a finance minister sees fit to impose no mater how harsh they may seem," Sriyan added.
Other analysts said history showed that in Thailand narrow political considerations of fractious coalition governments always overrode broad national economic interests.
That could inevitably lead to the downfall of the new finance minister and possibly of the administration in the future, they said.

"The finance job is not an easy one. That so many have left shows that in the present system the interests of politicians and their vested interests in business seems to be overriding national economic interests," said a senior vice-president of a financial institution.
"Unless politicians can display national interest instead of their own group interests we will see greater loss of foreign interest in Thailand," he said, declining to be identified.

Amnuay, a strong personality with sound credentials, quit after running into trouble with political strongmen from Chavalit's own New Aspiration Party and the Chart Pattana Party, the second largest in the ruling coalition.
He lost face when the cabinet, split by opposition from the Chart Pattana party, reversed his moves to raise excise taxes on some consumer goods.
Political sources said the change of finance minister could help ease political rivalries on economic matters within Chavalit's coalition for now.
Amnuay formulated some measures, including steep budget cuts, state rescue plans for crumbling financial institutions and stout defence of the embattled baht.
An analyst with a foreign investment bank said finance ministers also owed their existence to powerful bureaucrats who controlled implementing agencies.

"The financial measures needed to help Thailand out are there but it is a question of implementation. Unless bureaucrats who hold much sway in the current system also help the government implement them, the future looks bleak," he said.
